title: Horace Mann's Third-Quarter Core Earnings Jump 50% to $85.1 Million, the Strongest in Its History, as the Property and Casualty Combined Ratio Improves to 83.6% and Investment Losses Hold Net Income Flat
summary: Horace Mann Educators reported third-quarter 2026 core earnings of $85.1 million ($2.06 per share), up from $56.6 million, while net income was almost unchanged at $58.5 million because $20.6 million of after-tax investment losses offset the gain, and the company raised its full-year core earnings guidance to $5.75 to $5.95 per share.
description:
Horace Mann Educators Corporation released its third-quarter 2026 results on November 3, 2026, with a conference call the next day. The company sells auto, home, retirement and life products, with a focus on educators and school employees in the United States. This article reports the figures from the earnings release, which the company filed as an exhibit to a current report with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, and it marks where a figure has been calculated here rather than reported.

The headline: two measures, two directions

The release is built around the difference between net income and core earnings. Net income for the quarter was $58.5 million, or $1.41 per diluted share, against $58.3 million, or $1.40, in the third quarter of 2025. That is essentially flat. Core earnings, the measure the company uses to describe its underlying operating performance, were $85.1 million, or $2.06 per share, against $56.6 million, or $1.36. That is an increase of about 50.4%, and chief executive Marita Zuraitis said the company "delivered the strongest quarterly core earnings in our history."

The reason the two measures diverged is stated in the release. Net investment losses after tax were $20.6 million, or $0.50 per share, in the quarter, compared with net investment gains of $2.7 million, or $0.06 per share, a year earlier. The company reports non-core losses of $6.0 million in the quarter against $1.0 million a year earlier. The release reports these investment and other non-core items separately from core earnings, which is why core earnings moved up while net income stayed level. The release does not break down which securities produced the investment losses, so this article does not say more about them.

Nine-month picture

For the first nine months of 2026, net income was $141.3 million, or $3.43 per share, against $125.9 million, or $3.03, a year earlier, an increase of about 12% calculated here. Core earnings were $185.8 million, or $4.50 per share, against $145.5 million, or $3.50, up 27.7%. The nine-month trend therefore points the same way as the quarter, although the third quarter on its own showed a much larger gain in core earnings than in net income.

Revenue and investment income

Revenues were $439.2 million, against $438.5 million in the third quarter of 2025, a rise of 0.2%. For the nine months, revenues were $1,312.0 million, up 3.6%. Within the quarter, net investment income rose 17%, and premiums, contract charges and fee revenue rose 3%. The flat total therefore sits alongside growth in both of those lines. The release does not provide a bridge that reconciles each element to total revenue, so readers who want that should consult the full exhibit.

Property and casualty underwriting

The most concrete operating figure in the release is the property and casualty combined ratio, which was 83.6% for the quarter. The company says that is an improvement of nearly four points from a year earlier, which implies a prior-year ratio of roughly 87.5%, calculated here. A combined ratio below 100% means claims and expenses were lower than the premiums earned, so an 83.6% ratio indicates a substantial underwriting margin in the quarter. The release does not state the amount of catastrophe losses in the period, and it does not give separate auto and property ratios, so this article does not draw conclusions about how weather or claim costs contributed.

Guidance and returns

Horace Mann raised its full-year 2026 core earnings guidance to a range of $5.75 to $5.95 per share. The release does not give the prior range in the release, so the size of the increase cannot be stated here. Using the nine-month core figure of $4.50 per share, the range implies fourth-quarter core earnings of about $1.25 to $1.45 per share, calculated here by subtraction. That is below the $2.06 earned in the third quarter, which is a reminder that guidance is a company estimate and that quarterly results can vary.

On returns, trailing twelve-month core return on equity was 14.2%, against 13.8% a year earlier. Book value per share was $35.11, down 0.6%. Adjusted book value per share, which excludes the effect of unrealized gains and losses on fixed maturities, was $42.49, up 7.5%, and tangible book value per share was $37.85, up 9.4%.

How to read the comparison

There are three cautions for readers. First, core earnings are a non-GAAP measure defined by the company, and they are not directly comparable with the adjusted operating income measures used by other insurers. Second, a record quarter does not by itself show a trend, since one period can be affected by lower weather losses or favorable reserve changes. The release does not quantify either. Third, net income, which is the GAAP measure, was flat, and investors who focus on it will see a different quarter from those who focus on core earnings.

What the release does not say

The release does not include segment results for the supplemental and group, life or retirement businesses, so this article does not comment on them. It does not give catastrophe loss amounts, and it does not report share repurchase or dividend activity for the quarter. Anyone who wants those details should read the full exhibit and the company's filings.

What to watch

Three things stand out. The first is whether the combined ratio holds near the low-to-mid 80s once the seasonal pattern of weather claims is taken into account. The second is how much of the 17% rise in net investment income reflects higher yields rather than a larger portfolio, which the release does not separate. The third is how the investment losses evolve, since they were the reason net income did not follow core earnings upward. This article is a summary of public figures and is not investment advice.

Net income was $58.5 million ($1.41 per share) against $58.3 million ($1.40) because after-tax net investment losses of $20.6 million replaced a gain of $2.7 million.
The property and casualty combined ratio improved to 83.6%, nearly four points better than a year earlier, while revenues were $439.2 million, up 0.2%.

Full-year 2026 core earnings guidance was raised to $5.75 to $5.95 per share, and trailing core return on equity was 14.2% against 13.8%.
why_it_matters: Horace Mann sells auto, home, retirement and life products mainly to US educators, so its results offer a view of how a specialist carrier is performing as auto and home underwriting recovers. The quarter also shows why two earnings measures can move in opposite directions in the same period.

title: Radian's Third-Quarter Adjusted Operating EPS Rises 25% to $1.44 as the Inigo Acquisition Doubles Revenue to $624 Million, While Mortgage Delinquencies Edge Up to 2.68% and Buybacks Reach $379 Million This Year
summary: Radian Group reported third-quarter 2026 net income from continuing operations of $172 million ($1.28 per share) and adjusted diluted operating income of $1.44 per share, with revenue of $624 million after its Inigo acquisition, a mortgage delinquency rate of 2.68% and $379 million of share repurchases so far this year.
description:
Radian Group Inc. announced its third-quarter 2026 financial results on November 4, 2026, with a conference call on November 5. Radian is best known as a private mortgage insurer, which covers lenders against losses when borrowers who put down small deposits stop paying. This quarter's report is different from earlier ones because it includes a specialty insurance business following the company's acquisition of Inigo. This article reports figures from the company's press release and notes where a number has been calculated here rather than reported.

Earnings: headline and adjusted

Net income from continuing operations was $172 million, or $1.28 per diluted share, against $153 million, or $1.11, in the third quarter of 2025. That is an increase of about 12% calculated here. Total net income, which includes discontinued operations, was $164 million, or $1.22 per share, against $141 million, or $1.03. Pretax income from continuing operations was $228 million against $199 million.

On the adjusted basis the company uses to describe operations, adjusted pretax operating income was $254 million against $206 million, and adjusted diluted net operating income per share was $1.44 against $1.15, a rise of about 25% calculated here. Return on equity was 14.6% against 13.4%, and adjusted net operating return on equity was 16.3% against 13.9%. Adjusted measures are defined by the company and exclude certain items, so they should not be compared directly with other insurers' figures without checking the definitions.

Why revenue doubled

Total revenues were $624 million, compared with $303 million in the third quarter of 2025. The press release links the change to the Inigo acquisition, so the comparison is not like for like: the current quarter contains a business that was not in the prior-year figures. Readers who want to judge the underlying growth of the mortgage insurance franchise should look at the mortgage metrics below rather than at the revenue total.

The mortgage book

New insurance written, a measure of new business, was $14.7 billion in the quarter against $15.5 billion a year earlier, a decline of about 5% calculated here. Primary insurance in force, the total balance of loans covered, was $285.7 billion against $280.6 billion, a rise of about 2%. Persistency, the share of insurance that remains in force, was 83% against 84%.

The delinquency rate rose to 2.68% from 2.42%. That is still a small share of insured loans, but it is higher than a year ago, and it sits alongside the higher loss provision described below. The mortgage loss provision, the amount set aside for expected claims, was $176.9 million against $17.9 million. Within the mortgage segment, the company reported about $32 million of provision including $26 million of favorable development on prior periods, meaning that earlier estimates of loss were reduced. The Specialty segment accounted for about $148 million of the provision. These two components sum to slightly more than the $176.9 million total, and the release does not explain the difference in the figures cited here, so readers should consult the full tables for the reconciliation.

Combined ratios

The Mortgage combined ratio, which compares losses and expenses with premiums earned, was 36.6% against 27.0% a year earlier. A lower number is better, so the ratio worsened by about 9.6 points, calculated here, but it remains far below 100%, the level at which an insurer breaks even on underwriting. The Specialty combined ratio was 80.4%. There is no prior-year comparison for Specialty because the business was not part of Radian a year ago.

Capital: PMIERs

Private mortgage insurers must hold assets under the Private Mortgage Insurer Eligibility Requirements, known as PMIERs, to remain approved by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Radian reported available assets of $5.33 billion, against $5.96 billion a year earlier, and excess available assets above the requirement of $1.48 billion against $1.88 billion. The excess therefore fell by about $400 million, or roughly 21%, calculated here. The release does not say how much of that change came from the acquisition, from buybacks or from changes in the requirement, so this article does not attribute it.

Share repurchases and dividend

Radian repurchased $135 million of stock in the third quarter, or 3.7 million shares, and a further $117 million in October, or 3.5 million shares. For the year to date, repurchases were $379 million, about 8% of shares outstanding, and $484 million of authorization remained, expiring in December 2027. The quarterly dividend was $0.255 per share, or about $34 million. Together, the quarter's repurchases and dividend returned about $169 million to shareholders, calculated here.

Book value and accumulated losses

Book value per share was $35.78 against $34.34, an increase of 4.2%. Accumulated other comprehensive income was a loss of $3.32 per share against a loss of $1.67, which means unrealized losses on investments reduced book value by more than they did a year earlier. The release does not separate the causes.

What the release does not say

The release does not give guidance for the fourth quarter, does not break out the contribution of Inigo to adjusted income, and does not explain the reasons for the rise in delinquencies. This article therefore does not forecast or explain them.

What to watch

Three things stand out. The first is whether the delinquency rate continues to rise from 2.68%, since it feeds directly into future loss provisions. The second is how the PMIERs excess moves as the company continues to buy back shares. The third is how the Specialty segment contributes once a full year of comparison is available. This article is a summary of public figures and is not investment advice.

Total revenues were $624 million against $303 million a year earlier, reflecting the Inigo acquisition, and the mortgage loss provision was $176.9 million against $17.9 million, so quarterly results now include a specialty insurance business.

Radian's results are also the first in this series to show how a mortgage insurer reports after adding a specialty insurance line.

title: Primerica's Third-Quarter Diluted EPS Rises 6% to $6.76 as Record Investment Product Sales of $4.4 Billion Offset a 12% Drop in Term Life Segment Income and a Shrinking Sales Force
summary: Primerica reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $209.1 million and diluted earnings of $6.76 per share, as record investment and savings product sales of $4.4 billion lifted that segment's income 21% while Term Life segment income fell 12% to $152.7 million and the life-licensed sales force shrank 3% to 147,058.
description:
Primerica, Inc. released its third-quarter 2026 results on November 4, 2026, with an earnings webcast on November 5. The company sells term life insurance and investment and savings products to middle-income households in North America through a large network of independent representatives. This article reports the figures from the results release filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and notes where a number has been calculated here.

The headline numbers

Total revenues were $901.7 million, against $839.9 million in the third quarter of 2025, an increase of 7%. Income before income taxes was $271.9 million, essentially unchanged from $271.7 million. Net income was $209.1 million against $206.8 million, a rise of about 1%, and diluted earnings per share were $6.76 against $6.35, a rise of about 6% calculated here. The faster growth in per-share earnings reflects a lower share count: weighted average diluted shares fell to 30.8 million from 32.5 million because of share repurchases.

On the adjusted basis the company reports, adjusted net operating income was $209.3 million against $206.1 million, up 2%, and diluted adjusted operating earnings per share were $6.77 against $6.33, up 7%. The release notes that results include the annual actuarial assumption updates, which the company recognizes in the third quarter. The pre-tax gain from remeasurement of future policy benefits was $11.8 million against $23.1 million a year earlier, so that item contributed less to this year's quarter than to last year's. Return on stockholders' equity was 31.3%, and the adjusted return on adjusted stockholders' equity was 33.9%.

Term Life: revenue flat, income down

The Term Life Insurance segment is the company's largest. Adjusted operating revenues were $461.6 million against $463.3 million, effectively flat, but adjusted operating income before taxes fell about 12%, to $152.7 million from $172.7 million, a decline of $20.0 million calculated here. Adjusted direct premiums, a measure of premiums before reinsurance, rose 3% to $699.4 million, while reported net premiums were $453.6 million against $454.5 million.

New business was weaker. The face amount of term life insurance issued fell 5% to $25.7 billion from $27.1 billion, and the number of policies issued fell 7% to 73,813 from 79,379. Face amount in force was $969 billion. The release does not state the reasons for the lower segment income, so this article does not offer an explanation.

The sales force is smaller

Primerica's model depends on recruiting people to become licensed representatives. At the end of the quarter the life-licensed sales force was 147,058, down 3% from 152,200. Recruits were 90,818 against 101,156, down 10%, and new life-licensed representatives were 10,722 against 12,482, down 14%. Productivity, measured as average monthly policies issued per licensed representative, was 0.17, the same as a year earlier. With productivity unchanged, the 7% fall in policies issued is consistent with having fewer licensed representatives, though the release does not draw that connection explicitly and other factors may be involved.

Investment and Savings Products: a record

The Investment and Savings Products segment, had sales of $4.4 billion against $3.7 billion, up 19%, and the company described the figure as a record. Adjusted operating revenues rose 19% to $378.0 million, and adjusted operating income before taxes rose 21% to $114.1 million from $94.2 million. Client asset values at period end were $139.6 billion against $126.8 billion, up 10%, and net inflows were $407 million. The release does not separate how much of the revenue increase came from new sales and how much from other factors.

Corporate and Other Distributed Products had adjusted operating revenues of $62.2 million against $56.8 million, up 10%, and adjusted operating income before taxes of $5.3 million against $3.8 million. Closed brokered mortgage volume was $142.6 million against $143.4 million.

Capital and returns to stockholders

Primerica returned $159 million to stockholders in the quarter, made up of $122 million of share repurchases and $37 million of dividends. The board approved a dividend of $1.20 per share, payable on December 14, 2026 to stockholders of record on November 20, 2026. The estimated statutory risk-based capital ratio of Primerica Life Insurance Company was about 445% at September 30, 2026. Stockholders' equity was $2,826.6 million, up 16% from $2,445.9 million at December 31, 2025, while adjusted stockholders' equity, which removes the effect of unrealized gains and losses, was $2,496.5 million, up 4% from $2,400.6 million.

How to read the comparison

Two points are worth keeping in mind. First, the quarter's net income growth of 1% is smaller than the growth in per-share earnings of 6%, and the difference comes from buybacks rather than from the business growing faster. Second, the two main segments moved in opposite directions: income grew in Investment and Savings Products and fell in Term Life, so the total masks a shift in where earnings come from. Based on the segment figures, Investment and Savings Products income of $114.1 million is about 75% of Term Life income of $152.7 million, calculated here, up from about 55% a year earlier.

What the release does not say

The release does not include forward-looking financial guidance. It does not explain the decline in recruits or new licensees, and it does not give a view on demand for term life insurance in the market. CEO Glenn Williams attributed the quarter to consistent business fundamentals and an operating model aimed at middle-income families, and said stable Term Life earnings and record investment sales continue to drive earnings momentum.

What to watch

Three measures matter for the next few quarters: whether recruiting and the size of the sales force stabilize, whether policies issued recover, and whether Investment and Savings Products sales stay near the record level. This article is a summary of public figures and is not investment advice.

why_it_matters: Primerica sells term life insurance and investment products to middle-income families through a large network of part-time representatives, so its sales-force and policy counts are a read on demand for basic life cover. The quarter shows earnings growth coming from investment products while the insurance business shrinks slightly.

title: LIC's September-Quarter Standalone Profit Rises 20% to ₹12,076 Crore as Net Premium Income Climbs 16% to ₹1.47 Lakh Crore, With First-Half Value of New Business Up 34% and a Net Margin of 22.3%
summary: Life Insurance Corporation of India reported standalone net profit of ₹12,076 crore for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, up 20.1% from ₹10,053 crore, with net premium income of ₹1.47 lakh crore, first-half value of new business of ₹6,846 crore and a solvency ratio of 2.35, though profit fell 10.5% from the June quarter.
description:
Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) announced its financial results for the quarter and half-year ended September 30, 2026, which is the second quarter of the financial year 2026-27, in the first week of November 2026. This article is based on a report published by the Free Press Journal and updated on November 5, 2026, which gives the company's unaudited standalone figures. The report does not state the exact date of the board meeting, and this article has not reviewed LIC's own exchange filing, so readers who need exact figures should check that filing. Amounts are in Indian rupees, with one crore equal to ten million and one lakh crore equal to one trillion.

Profit: strong year on year, lower than the previous quarter

Standalone net profit for the quarter was ₹12,076.02 crore, up 20.1% from ₹10,053.39 crore in the same quarter of the previous year. Profit before tax was ₹12,125.82 crore against ₹10,146.97 crore. The report also notes that net profit was 10.5% lower than the ₹13,492.03 crore reported for the June quarter. For the half-year, standalone net profit was ₹25,568.05 crore, up 21.5% from ₹21,039.90 crore. The half-year figure equals the sum of the two quarters, and the percentage changes match the reported amounts, as checked here.

Other outlets have reported the quarterly profit as about ₹12,115 crore, a slightly different number from the ₹12,076 crore in this report. The article does not say why they differ, and this article uses the figure in the report it cites.

Premium income

Net premium income for the quarter was ₹1,47,018.18 crore, up 16.2% from ₹1,26,479.26 crore and up 15.5% from the June quarter. A headline that says "premium income rises 16%" refers to this quarterly figure. For the half-year, total premium income was ₹2,74,269 crore, up 11.6%, which is slower growth. Subtracting the second quarter from the half-year total gives about ₹1,27,251 crore for the first quarter, calculated here, which is consistent with the 15.5% sequential rise. It also implies slower growth in the first quarter than in the second, although the net and total premium measures may not be defined identically.

By product line, the report gives individual new business premium of ₹32,725 crore, up 14.9%, and group premium of ₹1,13,594 crore, up 19.6%. The report places these under the half-year heading but does not explicitly confirm the period, and their sum of about ₹1.46 lakh crore is close to the second-quarter net premium, so readers should confirm the period in LIC's filing before relying on them. The report also gives the number of individual policies sold as 70.97 lakh, down 2.25%. The count of policies fell while individual new business premium rose, but the two measures may cover different periods, so this article does not draw a conclusion from the contrast. LIC's share of first-year premium income for the half-year was 58.77%.

Investment income

Net investment income from policyholders' funds was ₹1,14,983.77 crore, up from ₹1,12,147.16 crore, a rise of about 2.5% calculated here. The report does not give total income, so the combined effect of premiums and investments on revenue cannot be stated from this source.

Value of new business and margins

For the first half of the financial year, LIC reported a value of new business (VNB) of ₹6,846 crore, up 34% from ₹5,111 crore. VNB is an actuarial estimate of the value created by policies sold in the period. The net VNB margin was 22.3%, up 470 basis points from 17.6%. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so 470 basis points is 4.7 percentage points. The overall expense ratio improved to 10.41% from 11.28%. The report does not explain what drove the margin change, such as product mix or pricing, and this article does not speculate.

Solvency and assets

The solvency ratio was 2.35, up from 2.13. The solvency ratio compares an insurer's available capital with the regulatory requirement, and the regulatory requirement for Indian insurers is a ratio of 1.5. Assets under management were ₹59.61 lakh crore, up 4.2%. The report does not state the period to which the solvency and asset figures relate, so they should be read as the latest figures reported with the results.

Other points in the report

LIC will adopt Indian Accounting Standards from April 1, 2027, subject to regulatory approval for a one-year deferment. The report also says Naga Nalini Kalluri was appointed Chief Compliance Officer with effect from November 6, 2026. It does not mention a dividend or the share price reaction, so this article does not report either.

How to read the results

Four cautions apply. First, the figures are unaudited. Second, year-on-year growth in profit of 20% sits beside a sequential fall of 10.5%, so the answer to whether profit is rising depends on which comparison is used. Third, premium growth is much higher in the quarter than in the half-year. Fourth, the margin and VNB figures are for the half-year and cannot be compared directly with the quarterly profit.

What to watch

The main measures to follow are whether the net VNB margin stays above the 22.3% reported for the half-year, how the solvency ratio develops, and what LIC says about the accounting-standards transition. This article is a summary of reported figures and is not investment advice.
source_name: Free Press Journal (report on LIC's Q2 FY27 unaudited results, updated November 5, 2026)

key_points: LIC's standalone net profit for the September 2026 quarter was ₹12,076.02 crore, up 20.1% from ₹10,053.39 crore, but down 10.5% from ₹13,492.03 crore in the June quarter.
Net premium income was ₹1,47,018.18 crore, up 16.2% from ₹1,26,479.26 crore, while first-half total premium income was ₹2,74,269 crore, up 11.6%, so the headline 16% applies to the quarter only.
First-half value of new business was ₹6,846 crore against ₹5,111 crore, up 34%, with the net margin at 22.3% against 17.6% and the overall expense ratio at 10.41% against 11.28%.
First-half standalone profit was ₹25,568.05 crore, up 21.5%, the solvency ratio was 2.35 against 2.13, and assets under management were ₹59.61 lakh crore, up 4.2%.

Individual policies sold were 70.97 lakh, down 2.25%, even though individual new business premium rose 14.9%, and LIC plans to adopt Indian Accounting Standards from April 1, 2027, subject to approval of a one-year deferment.
why_it_matters: LIC is India's largest life insurer and a major holder of Indian government and corporate securities, so its profit, premium and margin figures are widely used as a read on the life insurance sector. The quarter also shows why year-on-year and quarter-on-quarter comparisons can point in different directions.

title: Go Digit's September-Quarter Profit Falls 31% to ₹142 Crore as Insurance Service Expenses Rise 22% and the Combined Ratio Reaches 99.8%, With Flood Losses and Non-Renewals Weighing on a Business That Still Reports a 2.40 Solvency Ratio
summary: Go Digit General Insurance reported a September-quarter FY27 net profit of about ₹142 crore, down 31% from ₹206.8 crore, as insurance service expenses rose 22% against 1.7% revenue growth, the combined insurance service ratio reached 99.8% including flood losses, gross written premium fell 3.6% and the solvency ratio stood at 2.40.
description:
Go Digit General Insurance, a listed Indian general insurer, reported lower profit for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, the second quarter of the financial year 2026-27. This article is based on two news reports dated November 5, 2026, from Inc42 and Multibagg. Neither report quotes management, and this article has not reviewed the company's exchange filing, so readers who need exact figures should consult it. The reports contain figures that do not reconcile with each other, and those gaps are noted below rather than smoothed over. Amounts are in Indian rupees, with one crore equal to ten million.

Profit: down sharply

Inc42 reports net profit of ₹142.4 crore for the quarter, down 31.1% from ₹206.8 crore in the second quarter of FY26. Profit before tax was ₹190.18 crore against ₹276.30 crore. Compared with the first quarter of FY27, when net profit was ₹378.61 crore, the second-quarter figure is down 62.4%. For the half-year, net profit was ₹521 crore, down 3.2% from ₹538.23 crore, and the two quarters add up to that figure, as checked here. The first quarter's profit was much higher than the second's, which is why the half-year decline is much smaller than the quarterly one.

Multibagg reports a different headline measure. It gives profit after tax excluding mark-to-market movements as ₹208 crore, down 29% year on year, and describes profit from continuing operations as ₹142.39 crore. It does not explain the gap between the two figures, and it does not state the prior-year figure for the ₹208 crore measure. Readers should therefore be careful not to compare the ₹208 crore figure with the ₹142.4 crore figure as though they measured the same thing.

Revenue and premium

Insurance revenue was ₹2,720.5 crore, up 1.7% from ₹2,674.9 crore and up 2.1% from the previous quarter. Gross written premium, the total premium booked, fell 3.6% to ₹2,571 crore. Gross direct premium income was ₹2,351 crore and fell 1.2%. Within revenue, the largest segment was motor third party, at ₹1,066.1 crore, up 8.3%, followed by motor own damage at ₹640.64 crore, up 11.4%.

Multibagg says gross written premium excluding health reinsurance and government health business was flat, and attributes this to management's decision not to renew unattractively priced business. The report does not give the amounts excluded, so the size of that adjustment cannot be checked. It does indicate that part of the fall in premium was a choice rather than lost demand, but the report offers no data on how much.

Underwriting: where the profit went

The main driver of lower profit was the insurance service result, which Inc42 reports at ₹43 crore, down 73.4% from ₹161.98 crore a year earlier and down 62.3% from ₹114 crore in the previous quarter. Insurance service expenses rose 22.4% to ₹2,607.73 crore from ₹2,130.85 crore, far faster than the 1.7% growth in revenue. Incurred claims were ₹1,968.03 crore, up 9.2%. Commission expenses were ₹781.88 crore, down 2.6%.

Multibagg reports that the combined insurance service ratio, a measure of claims and expenses against revenue, was 99.8%, or 97.4% excluding a flood loss. A ratio below 100% indicates an underwriting profit before investment income, so the business was close to break-even on underwriting. Excluding the flood loss, the ratio is 2.4 percentage points lower, calculated here. The total claims ratio was 62.4% against 58.6% in FY26. By line, the motor claims ratio was 58.4%, with 80.3% for own damage and 45.2% for third party. For the half-year, the combined ratio was 98.4%. The report says that after the first quarter management had expected the own-damage loss ratio to stabilize in the second quarter after corrective action in its car portfolio, and it does not say whether that happened. Multibagg gives no prior-year quarterly ratio, so it is not possible to say from these reports whether the ratio rose or fell year on year.

Investment income

Investment income was ₹368.4 crore, up 20.6% from ₹305.5 crore but down 39.2% from ₹606.47 crore in the previous quarter. The net finance result was ₹196.94 crore, up 28.6% year on year. Investment income cushioned the quarter compared with underwriting, but it was well below the level of the first quarter, which is consistent with the large quarter-on-quarter profit fall.

Balance sheet

The solvency ratio was 2.40, against a regulatory requirement of 1.50. Assets under management were ₹24,371 crore, up 15.9%, and net worth under Indian accounting standards was ₹8,137 crore.

Figures that do not reconcile

Inc42's reported figures contain several gaps. Insurance revenue of ₹2,720.5 crore less expenses of ₹2,607.73 crore would give about ₹113 crore, not the reported insurance service result of ₹43 crore. The four expense components it lists add up to about ₹2,940 crore, well above the ₹2,607.73 crore total, possibly because of different bases, but the report does not say. And the insurance service result of ₹43 crore plus the net finance result of ₹196.94 crore comes to about ₹240 crore, against reported profit before tax of ₹190.18 crore. These gaps are not explained in the report, so this article treats the individual figures as reported and does not rely on any derived total.

Share price and what is missing

Inc42 says the shares closed 1.05% higher at ₹260.30 that day. Neither report includes a management explanation beyond the points above, and neither gives a dividend or guidance.

What to watch

Readers may watch whether the claims ratio in motor own damage improves, whether premium growth returns once the non-renewal of weaker-priced business has passed, and how investment income behaves after its drop from the first quarter. This article is a summary of news reports and is not investment advice.

title: Great Eastern's Third-Quarter Net Profit Falls 72% to S$102.9 Million on Investment Losses and a S$57.1 Million Loss on the Part-Sale of Its Indonesian Unit, While Core Insurance Profit Rises 6% and New Business Value Climbs 14%
summary: Great Eastern Holdings reported third-quarter 2026 net profit of S$102.9 million, down 72% from S$372 million, as an investment loss and a S$57.1 million one-off loss on the part-sale of its Indonesian life unit outweighed a 6% rise in core insurance profit to S$179.3 million and a 14% rise in new business embedded value to S$208.2 million.
description:
Great Eastern Holdings reported its third-quarter and nine-month 2026 results on November 2, 2026, for the period ended September 30. The figures in this article come from a report that cites the company's media release on the Singapore Exchange, as well as coverage by The Business Times. This article has not reviewed the exchange filing itself, so readers who need exact figures should consult it. Amounts are in Singapore dollars unless stated otherwise.

The headline: profit down, core earnings up

Net profit for the third quarter was S$102.9 million, down 72% from S$372 million in the third quarter of 2025. Over the same quarter, core insurance profit rose 6% to S$179.3 million from S$169.2 million. Net profit also reflects investment results and the effect of a corporate transaction, both described below.

The report states that profit from the insurance business fell 35% to S$148.5 million. It does not give the prior-year figure, which would be about S$228 million if the 35% decline is exact, calculated here. Investment profit in the insurance fund swung to a loss of S$30.8 million from a profit of S$59.6 million. In the shareholders' fund, the result swung to a loss of S$45.6 million from a profit of S$143.2 million. The report does not provide a full reconciliation between the core result and net profit.

The Indonesian divestment

During the quarter, the group sold part of PT Great Eastern Life Indonesia, known as GELI, to OCBC Indonesia. The transaction closed on September 1, 2026, and the report says it was carried out to meet Indonesian ownership rules. After that date Great Eastern no longer controls GELI. The sale produced a one-off loss of S$57.1 million. A reclassification gain of S$52.6 million recognized in other comprehensive income largely offsets it, and the company says the effect on total comprehensive income is broadly neutral. The net of the two amounts is a loss of S$4.5 million, calculated here. The Singapore life company, The Great Eastern Life Assurance Company Limited, remains part of the group.

New business

Total weighted new sales, a measure that counts regular premiums in full and single premiums at a fraction of their value, were S$362.4 million, down 3% from S$373.1 million. In Singapore, weighted new sales were S$238.1 million against S$251.9 million, a decline of about 5% calculated here. In Malaysia they were S$117.0 million against S$113.3 million, an increase of about 3%. The two markets add up to S$355.1 million, leaving about S$7.3 million, calculated here, from other operations that the report does not itemize.

New business embedded value, an estimate of the value created by new policies sold, was S$208.2 million, up 14% from S$182.2 million. Sales therefore fell while the estimated value of the business written rose, which is consistent with a higher value per dollar of sales; the report describes the nine-month improvement as reflecting a more favorable and diversified product mix. It does not provide a separate explanation for the quarter.

Nine-month results

For the first nine months of 2026, net profit was S$952.4 million, down 1% from S$965.7 million. Core insurance profit was S$742.7 million, up 22% from S$609.8 million. Total weighted new sales were S$1,175.6 million, up 9%, and new business embedded value was S$613.5 million, up 23% from S$498.7 million. The year to date therefore looks much steadier than the third quarter alone: net profit is nearly level and core earnings and new business value are both higher. The nine-month decline of about S$13.3 million, calculated here, is far smaller than the S$269.1 million fall in the third quarter, which implies that net profit in the first half was higher than a year earlier.

Outlook and what the report does not say

Management said the investment outlook is likely to remain challenging in the near to medium term. The report does not give an operating profit figure, so core insurance profit is the nearest equivalent, and it does not provide the prior-year figure for profit from the insurance business. It does not give guidance for the fourth quarter. Some outlets quote a US dollar figure of about US$80.4 million for the quarter's profit, which is a conversion of the S$102.9 million rather than a separate number.

How to read the results

There are three points to keep in mind. First, core insurance profit and net profit measure different things, and the gap this quarter coincided with an investment loss and the Indonesian transaction. Second, the divestment loss is described by the company as largely offset elsewhere in comprehensive income, so it should not be read as a loss of S$57.1 million in value. Third, new sales and new business value moved in different directions, so which measure matters depends on whether the question is about volume or value.

What to watch

Readers following the group should watch investment results in the next quarter, whether sales in Singapore recover from the decline, and how the group reports earnings now that GELI is outside its control. This article is a summary of reported figures and is not investment advice.
